title: Arizona tree rings show a regular 150-year climate periodicity

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Arizona tree rings show a regular 150-year climate periodicity

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Century-smoothed annual ring widths of Arizona yellow pines show that the climate of Arizona over the past 500 years fluctuated with a regular period of almost exactly 150 years, probably mainly in moisture rather than temperature.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: from which we seem compelled to draw the direct conclusion that the climate of Arizona, during the last 500 years, has fluctuated with a regular periodicity of almost precisely 150 years.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter III, “The Rate of Growth”; topic “Seasonal fluctuations of growth”. Scope: Arizona climate, 1390s–1910s, inferred from ponderosa (yellow) pine rings

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch03-24: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.93

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The period, location, proxy, and time window define a direct test. Public tree-ring archives have the necessary raw measurements and long chronology, while modern spectral methods can quantify uncertainty and distinguish periodicity from autocorrelated variability.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Construct Arizona ponderosa-pine ring-width chronologies for the stated interval, remove age trends, and test for a stable approximately 150-year spectral peak against red-noise and nonstationary alternatives. Compare the chronology with independent moisture and temperature reconstructions to identify the climatic correlate.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Only about three cycles occur in a 500-year window.

Detrending and smoothing choices can create or suppress low-frequency peaks.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The stated evidence is ponderosa ring width, and those series are openly archived at far higher replication than the few trees Thompson smoothed. Standard spectral tests can accept or reject a stable 150-year line. Discriminating power stays moderate because century smoothing and red noise can imitate a long cycle, and because moisture rather than temperature was an inference from the regional climate rather than a separate measurement.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: On Arizona ponderosa ring-width chronologies, compare a red-noise spectrum of the raw series and of 100-year smoothed means against a stable peak near 150 years over roughly 1390–1910, then repeat the test on an independent summer-drought reconstruction. A significant, stable 150-year peak would support the claim; a featureless continuum, or a peak that appears only after century smoothing, would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Ring width mixes moisture, temperature and stand dynamics.

The gridded drought product used here is densest after 1700, so the early part of Thompson's interval rests mainly on the ring measurements.

A 500-year window contains only about three cycles, and 100-year smoothing can impose a smooth wave.

fields.label: Hypothesis
fields.value: Annual ring-width chronologies of Arizona ponderosa pine over roughly 1390-1910 contain a regular oscillation with a period of about 150 years, visible as a significant spectral peak near 150 yr and as century-smoothed maxima recurring every ~150 yr.

fields.label: Method
fields.value: Downloaded the two Tucson-format .crn chronologies from NCEI, parsed the standard index (x1000, 9990 = missing) and sample depth, and took 1390-1910 (az572, 521 yr, complete) and 1420-1910 (az547, 491 yr). Test 1: raw periodogram of the mean-removed index against 5000 AR(1) surrogates matched in lag-1 autocorrelation (0.45, 0.52) and variance; the largest ordinate at 120-200 yr was compared with the pointwise 95th percentile (and with a band-maximum null). Test 2: 101-yr centred running mean (51-yr as sensitivity); local maxima at least 50 yr apart; intervals between successive maxima.

fields.label: Pass criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered. Primary series: ITRDB chronology az572 (Flagstaff, Arizona, Pinus ponderosa, 'Modern + Archaeological', AD 570-1987), the standard index over the window 1390-1910 (521 yr). Replicate: ITRDB az547 (Walnut Canyon, Pinus ponderosa, 1420-1987) over 1420-1910. Test 1 (spectral): periodogram of the mean-removed annual index; null = AR(1) with the series' lag-1 autocorrelation and variance, 5000 surrogates; pass if the largest periodogram ordinate at periods 120-200 yr exceeds the pointwise 95th percentile of the surrogate periodograms and its period lies in 130-170 yr. Test 2 (regularity of century-smoothed maxima, Douglass's own procedure): 101-yr centred running mean of the index (using data from 1340 on so the smoothed series spans 1390-1910); find local maxima of the smoothed series separated by at least 50 yr; pass if there are at least two intervals between successive maxima and every interval lies in 125-175 yr. Supports if both tests pass on az572.

fields.label: Fail criterion
fields.value: Refutes if both tests fail on az572 (no significant 120-200-yr spectral peak against red noise, and smoothed maxima spaced irregularly or outside 125-175 yr). Mixed if exactly one test passes, or if az572 passes but the az547 replicate fails both tests.

fields.label: Unit
fields.value: yr, mean interval between successive maxima of the 101-yr-smoothed Flagstaff index 1390-1910 (intervals 73, 57, 70, 68, 109); strongest 120-200-yr periodogram ordinate at 174 yr has power 1.33 vs AR(1) 95th percentile 1.64

fields.label: Uncertainty
fields.value: 521-yr window holds ~3.5 cycles of 150 yr; spectral test low-powered by design, so the smoothed-maxima test was pre-registered alongside

fields.label: Interpretation
fields.value: Thompson relayed Douglass's (1909, 1914) reading of century-smoothed Flagstaff pine ring widths as showing a ~150-yr climatic cycle. 'Regular period of almost exactly 150 years' is read as a spectral line in the 130-170-yr band that is significant against a red-noise background, together with smoothed maxima recurring at 150 +/- 25 yr. The moisture-versus-temperature attribution is not tested. Modern ITRDB chronologies are standardized indices (age trend removed) built from many trees, not the few raw series Douglass had; they are the best available record of the same trees' growth signal. A 521-yr window holds only ~3.5 cycles of 150 yr, so the spectral test is low-powered and is complemented by the smoothed-maxima test.

fields.label: Datasets
fields.value:
ITRDB chronology az572, Flagstaff Modern+Archaeological, Pinus ponderosa (Dean & Robinson), AD 570-1987

ITRDB chronology az547, Walnut Canyon, Pinus ponderosa (Graybill), AD 1420-1987

fields.label: Caveats
fields.value:
Both pre-registered tests fail at both sites: no 120-200-yr spectral ordinate exceeds the red-noise 95th percentile (Flagstaff 174 yr: 1.33 vs 1.64; Walnut Canyon 164 yr: 2.21 vs 3.39), and century-smoothed maxima recur every 57-133 yr (means 75 and 89 yr), not every 150. The smoothed series do oscillate, but irregularly and roughly twice as fast as Thompson's figure; a 51-yr smoothing gives the same conclusion.

Sample depth is thin early in the window (Flagstaff: 1-3 trees before 1400, 3-6 in the 1400s; Walnut Canyon: 2-4 trees before 1600), so the 15th-16th-century part of the index is noisy; this weakens any periodicity test but cannot create a regular 150-yr cycle where none is detected.

ITRDB standard chronologies remove the age trend by curve fitting; Douglass smoothed raw widths of a few trees. Detrending with conservative curves preserves century-scale variance in most chronologies but could damp a very long oscillation; the 521-yr window itself limits detectable periods to well under ~260 yr for two cycles.

Not pre-registered, reported as observation only: both sites show a ~70-yr spectral peak (Walnut Canyon 70 yr at 2.4x the AR(1) 95th percentile; Flagstaff 74 yr at 1.4x), in the range of known multidecadal drought variability in the Southwest, not the 150-yr cycle claimed.

The moisture-versus-temperature attribution in the claim was not tested.
